## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.87380.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.87380.3.sa3)

Original review

This study investigates the hypothesis that humans (but not non-human primates) spontaneously learn reversible temporal associations (i.e., learning a B-A association after only being exposed to A-B sequences), which the authors consider to be a foundational property of symbolic cognition. To do so, they expose humans and macaques to 2-item sequences (in a visual-auditory experiment, pairs of images and spoken nonwords, and in a visual-visual experiment, pairs of images and abstract geometric shapes) in a fixed temporal order, then measure the brain response during a test phase to congruent vs. incongruent pairs (relative to the trained associations) in canonical vs. reversed order (relative to the presentation order used in training). The advantage of neuroimaging for this question is that it removes the need for a behavioral test, which non-human primates can fail for reasons unrelated to the cognitive construct being investigated. In humans, the researchers find statistically indistinguishable incongruity effects in both directions (supporting a spontaneous reversible association), whereas in monkeys they only find incongruity effects in the canonical direction (supporting an association but a lack of spontaneous reversal). Although the precise pattern of activation varies by experiment type (visual-auditory vs. visual-visual) in both species, the authors point out that some of the regions involved are also those that are most anatomically different between humans and other primates. The authors interpret their findings to support the hypothesis that reversible associations, and by extension symbolic cognition, is uniquely human.

This study is a valuable complement to prior behavioral work on this question. However, I have some concerns about methods and framing.

Methods - Design issues:

(1) The authors originally planned to use the same training/testing protocol for both species but the monkeys did not learn anything, so they dramatically increased the amount of training and evaluation. By my calculation from the methods section, humans were trained on 96 trials and tested on 176, whereas the monkeys got an additional 3,840 training trials and 1,408 testing trials. The authors are explicit that they continued training the monkeys until they got a congruity effect. On the one hand, it is commendable that they are honest about this in their write-up, given that this detail could easily be framed as deliberate after the fact. On the other hand, it is still a form of p-hacking, given that it's critical for their result that the monkeys learn the canonical association (otherwise, the critical comparison to the non-canonical association is meaningless).

(2) Between-species comparisons are challenging. In addition to having differences in their DNA, human participants have spent many years living in a very different culture than that of NHPs, including years of formal education. As a result, attributing the observed differences to biology is challenging. One approach that has been adopted in some past studies is to examine either young children or adults from cultures that don't have formal educational structures. This is not the approach the authors take. This major confound needs to minimally be explicitly acknowledged up front.

(3) Humans have big advantages in processing and discriminating spoken stimuli and associating them to visual stimuli (after all, this is what words are in spoken human languages). Experiment 2 ameliorates these concerns to some degree, but still it is difficult to attribute the failure of NHPs to show reversible associations in Experiment 1 to cognitive differences rather than the relative importance of sound string to meaning associations in the human vs. NHP experiences.

(4) More minor: The localizer task (math sentences vs. other sentences) makes sense for math but seems to make less sense for language: why would a language region respond more to sentences that don't describe math vs. ones that do?

Methods - Analysis issues:

(5) The analyses appear to "double dip" by using the same data to define the clusters and to statistically test the average cluster activation (Kriegeskorte et al., 2009). The resulting effect sizes are therefore likely inflated, and the p-values are anticonservative.

FRAMING:

(6) The framing ("Brain mechanisms of reversible symbolic reference: A potential singularity of the human brain") is bigger than the finding (monkeys don't spontaneously reverse a temporal association but humans do). The title and discussion are full of buzzy terms ("brain mechanisms", "symbolic", and "singularity") that are only connected to the experiments by a debatable chain of assumptions.

First, this study shows relatively little about brain "mechanisms" of reversible symbolic associations, which implies insights about how these associations are learned, recognized, and represented. But we're only given standard fMRI analyses that are quite inconsistent across similar experimental paradigms, with purely suggestive connections between these spatial patterns and prior work on comparative brain anatomy.

Second, it's not clear what the relationship is between symbolic cognition and a propensity to spontaneously reverse a temporal association. Certainly if there are inter-species differences in learning preferences this is important to know about, but why is this construed as a difference in the presence or absence of symbols? Because the associations aren't used in any downstream computation, there is not even any way for participants to know which is the sign and which is the signified: these are merely labels imposed by the researchers on a sequential task.

Third, the word "singularity" is both problematically ambiguous and not well supported by the results. "Singularity" is a highly loaded word that the authors are simply using to mean "that which is uniquely human". Rather than picking a term with diverse technical meanings across fields and then trying to restrict the definition, it would be better to use a different term. Furthermore, even under the stated definition, this study performed a single pairwise comparison between humans and one other species (macaques), so it is a stretch to then conclude (or insinuate) that the "singularity" has been found (see also pt. 2 above).

(7) Related to pt. 6, there is circularity in the framing whereby the authors say they are setting out to find out what is uniquely human, hypothesizing that the uniquely human thing is symbols, and then selecting a defining trait of symbols (spontaneous reversible association) *because* it seems to be uniquely human (see e.g., "Several studies previously found behavioral evidence for a uniquely human ability to spontaneously reverse a learned association (Imai et al., 2021; Kojima, 1984; Lipkens et al., 1988; Medam et al., 2016; Sidman et al., 1982), and such reversibility was therefore proposed as a defining feature of symbol representation reference (Deacon, 1998; Kabdebon and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2019; Nieder, 2009).", line 335). They can't have it both ways. Either "symbol" is an independently motivated construct whose presence can be independently tested in humans and other species, or it is by fiat synonymous with the "singularity". This circularity can be broken by a more modest framing that focuses on the core research question (e.g., "What is uniquely human? One possibility is spontaneous reversal of temporal associations.") and then connects (speculatively) to the bigger conceptual landscape in the discussion ("Spontaneous reversal of temporal associations may be a core ability underlying the acquisition of mental symbols").

Comments on revised version:

I thank the authors for engaging constructively with my comments. I'm convinced by the responses to my original points 1, 2, 3, and 4. I'm also partially convinced by the response to point 6 (with qualifications discussed below). I do want to clear the record on points 1 and 6 (about which the authors expressed offense at aspects of my original comments), and to press on points 5 and 7.

(1) It's very helpful to know that the plan was always to extend training in Expt 1. The rationale is now clear in the methods, although I'd encourage the authors to also emphasize this if space permits in the vicinity of lines 211-216, which still read as if the extended training was a post hoc decision ("the canonical congruity effect... was not significant... after 3 days of exposure... Thus... monkeys were further exposed..."). The authors have objected to my original use of "p hacking", which I agree was too strong (my apologies). My intention was only to point out that *if it were the case that training duration was conditional on the monkeys' success at learning the canonical association* (which the authors have now clarified was not the case), then this would be steering the study post hoc to achieve a desired outcome. I recognize the authors' point that the canonical direction was a sanity check, not the effect of interest (reversed association), but it's still true that they needed to achieve this sanity check in order for the absence of a reversed effect to be meaningful. This was the source of my original concern. This point is only clarificational (no action is recommended).

(5) The authors have said they don't understand my concern about "double-dipping" in the statistical analyses, so I will attempt to clarify. First, I should stress that this concern applies only to the whole-brain results (Tables 1-4), not the fROI results. As the authors point out, this was indeed unclear, and I apologize. My concern about Tables 1-4 is that they seem to be derived using the classical technique of thresholding contrasts at some significance level to define clusters and then reporting cluster statistics (in this case, t-values) derived from *the same contrast in the same activation maps*. If this is not what was done (i.e., if orthogonal data and/or contrasts were used to define clusters and quantify contrasts within clusters, as in the fROI analyses), then this point is moot (and clarification in the paper would be helpful). But if this is what was done, then this procedure is known to be distortionary (e.g., Kriegeskorte et al 2009, "Nonindependent selective analysis is incorrect and should not be acceptable in neuroscientific publications").

(6) The authors have objected to my use of the term "insinuate" as pejorative. I don't share this impression (and insult was certainly not my intent) but I'm happy to concede that a less loaded term (e.g., "suggest") would have been a better choice. I apologize. In any case, I stand by my intended original concern that a key idea in this piece (that reversible symbolic inference is a singularity of the human brain) is being advanced rhetorically rather than empirically, by repeatedly supplying it to readers (albeit with qualifiers like "potential") as an interpretive lens through which to view empirical results that only directly support a more modest claim (that macaques spontaneously reverse sequential associations less readily than humans do). To be clear, it is good that the authors don't make this stronger claim outright, and it is fine to motivate a more modest research question (e.g., do species differ in spontaneous reversal of associations) on the grounds that it is a stepping stone to a bigger one (what is the singularity). But by placing the bigger framing front and center in this way, there's a risk that this paper will be received by the community as establishing a conclusion that it does not actually establish.

(7) The authors have said they don't understand the circularity I'm alleging. Having read the revision, I believe the issue is still there, so I'll make another attempt. The problem is most clearly apparent in the Discussion text quoted in my original comment (lines 347-350 of the revision, emphasis mine): "Several studies previously found behavioural evidence for a *uniquely human* ability to spontaneously reverse a learned association (Imai et al., 2021; Kojima, 1984; Lipkens et al., 1988; Medam et al., 2016; Sidman et al., 1982), and such reversibility was *therefore* proposed as a defining feature of symbol representation reference (Deacon, 1998; Kabdebon and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2019; Nieder, 2009)." In other words, reversal of associations is selected as a defining feature of symbols and targeted by this study *because* it is thought to be uniquely human. This is fine, but it prohibits you from then advocating the hypothesis that symbolic cognition is the singularity (lines 49-52), because "symbol" is being defined such that this is necessarily the case. To minimally paraphrase what I perceive to be the circular logic in the framing, the argument seems to go: "What is uniquely human? Symbols. What are symbols? That which is uniquely human." In my original comment, I suggested a reframing that would fix this issue, namely: "What is uniquely human? Spontaneous reversal of temporal associations." The authors say they don't see the difference between this framing and their own, so I'll try to clarify: the difference is that it sidesteps the notion of "symbol", and in so doing removes the circular definitions of "symbol" and "singularity" in terms of each other. This suggestion was given not as a prescription but as an example to show that the issue can be remedied by revisions to the framing without doing damage to the empirical claims. If the authors prefer a different remedy that avoids circular definitions of terms, that's fine.

claims.evidence: This is a critical evaluation of prior research methods.

claims.claim: The current study used fMRI and a passive paradigm to directly probe whether any area of the monkey brain would exhibit surprise at a violation of the reversal of a learned association.

claims.claim: The present work provides a simple experimental paradigm that can easily be extended to test whether humans are unique in their ability to acquire symbols.

results.result: In Experiment 1 (audio-visual pairs), humans showed spontaneous bidirectional reversal of learned associations. After learning unidirectional associations, humans exhibited surprise signals (violation-of-expectation responses) to incongruent pairings in both the learned (canonical) and reversed directions. These effects occurred within an extended bilateral network including the multiple-demand system (IFG, MFG, AI, IPS, dACC), language network (left STS), and precuneus, with no significant interaction between congruity and canonicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C6, C35-C39, C41-C42 collectively demonstrate that humans spontaneously reverse learned associations. The fMRI data (n=31) show significant activation (p<0.001 voxel, p<0.05 cluster corrected) for incongruent trials in both canonical and reversed directions across a broad bilateral network. Critically, the absence of a congruity × canonicity interaction (C41) provides statistical evidence that the reversal effect is equivalent to the learned direction effect, directly supporting the reversibility hypothesis.

results.result: In Experiment 1 (audio-visual pairs), monkeys showed learned associations only in the canonical direction without spontaneous reversal. After initial training (24 trials/pair) showed no learning, extended training (~960 trials/pair over 2 weeks) produced congruity effects confined to early visual areas (V1, V2, V4) and auditory association areas in the canonical direction only. A significant interaction between congruity and canonicity confirmed that learned associations did not reverse in monkeys.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C8, C43-C48 demonstrate that monkeys learned associations but did not reverse them. The fMRI data (n=2 monkeys, 12 scan sessions) show significant canonical congruity effects (p<0.001, cluster p<0.05) restricted to sensory areas, with no significant clusters in the reversed direction and a significant congruity × canonicity interaction in V2 and V4. This provides both positive evidence of learning and negative evidence (with statistical confirmation via interaction) of non-reversal.

results.result: In Experiment 2 (visual-visual pairs with reward), monkeys showed enhanced learning with prefrontal involvement but still no spontaneous reversal. With reward association, significant canonical congruity effects emerged after minimal training (24 trials/pair) in visual areas (V1, V2, V4), prefrontal cortex (45B, 46v), area 6, and STS. However, congruity effects remained restricted to the learned direction with significant interaction between congruity and canonicity, and effects were present only for high-reward conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C58 show that reward motivation enhanced learning speed and recruited prefrontal areas but did not enable reversal. The fMRI data (n=3 monkeys, first imaging day after training) demonstrate significant canonical congruity effects with prefrontal involvement, no significant reversed congruity effects, and a significant congruity × canonicity interaction. The reward-specific effect (C57) with significant interaction in area 45 and caudate provides additional mechanistic insight. This comprehensively addresses potential confounds about motivation and attention.

results.result: In Experiment 2 (visual-visual pairs), humans again showed spontaneous reversal of learned associations, though with reduced language network involvement. The main congruity effect was significant in a network similar to Experiment 1 (bilateral MFG, left IPS, bilateral AI, dACC, left IT), with limited STS involvement. Crucially, no interaction between congruity and canonicity was found, indicating full reversibility even with visual symbols.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 demonstrate that reversibility in humans extends beyond auditory-linguistic stimuli to visual symbols. The fMRI data (n=24) show significant congruity effects in both canonical and reversed directions (p<0.001 voxel, p<0.05 cluster corrected) with no significant interaction at standard or lower thresholds (p<0.01). The reduced language network involvement (C61) while maintaining reversibility supports the interpretation that this is a general symbolic capacity rather than language-specific.

results.result: Joint analysis of both human experiments revealed a broad bilateral network for reversible symbolic associations across modalities. A main congruity effect was observed in bilateral insula, MFG, precentral, IPS, precuneus, ACC, and STS in both canonical and reversed directions, with no region showing a congruity × canonicity interaction. Only left posterior STS showed modality-specific differences (larger in audio-visual than visual-visual paradigm).
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C70 from the joint analysis (n=55) provide strong evidence for a modality-general reversible symbolic network. The absence of congruity × canonicity interaction across the whole brain confirms reversibility is consistent across experiments. The single region (left pSTS) showing experiment differences (C69) with specific coordinates and statistics ([−60 −40 8], z=4.51, pcor=0.049) suggests language-specific contributions are limited and localized, supporting the broader symbolic network interpretation.

results.result: ROI analysis using independent localizers confirmed main congruity effects across all language and mathematical ROIs, with modality-specific effects limited to posterior STS and IFG triangularis. Importantly, no ROI showed significant canonicity × congruity or experiment × canonicity × congruity interactions, confirming whole-brain findings of full reversibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C74 from the ROI analysis (n=52) provide convergent evidence using an independent, subject-specific approach. The main congruity effect across all ROIs (C71) with no reversibility interactions (C74) confirms the whole-brain results. The specific congruity × experiment interaction only in pSTS and IFG triangularis (C73) for linguistic symbols provides precise anatomical specificity for language contributions while confirming other areas support general symbolic processing.

results.result: Behavioral familiarity ratings in Experiment 2 confirmed spontaneous reversal in humans. Although congruent canonical pairs were rated more familiar than congruent reversed pairs (t(20)=2.8, p=0.01), both were rated much more familiar than incongruent or never-seen pairs (all t(20)>7, p<0.0001). A behavioral reversibility index correlated with fMRI congruity effects in left area 44 (canonical: r=0.49, p=0.028; reversed: r=0.64, p=0.002) and right cerebellum (reversed only: r=0.57, p=0.008).
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C79 provide behavioral validation of the fMRI findings. The familiarity ratings (C77-C78) demonstrate that humans experience a 'memory illusion' for reversed pairs despite their low presentation frequency (10%), with large effect sizes (t>7). The brain-behavior correlations (C75-C76) link individual differences in behavioral reversibility to neural responses, particularly for reversed trials, strengthening the interpretation that the fMRI effects reflect genuine symbolic reversal rather than artifacts.

results.result: Experiment 1 successfully established the experimental paradigm with appropriate sensory controls. Humans (n=31) and monkeys (n=2) were exposed to four audio-visual pairs over 3 days (24 trials/pair), with two pairs in each temporal direction. During fMRI testing, the design included 70% congruent canonical, 10% incongruent canonical, 10% congruent reversed, and 10% incongruent reversed trials. Visual and auditory stimuli could be temporally separated in the fMRI data, with appropriate timing of responses in visual and auditory cortices.
results.evaluation: Claims C27-C34 describe the experimental design and basic sensory validation. The temporal separation of visual and auditory responses (C31-C32) demonstrated by hemodynamic response timing (Figure 1D-E) confirms the paradigm can dissociate the two stimuli within pairs. The weak auditory response in monkeys (C33) is acknowledged and explained by anatomical differences (C34), with appropriate citations. The design is well-controlled with balanced presentation directions (C28) to avoid confounding temporal order reversal with novelty.

results.result: In humans, no congruity effects were found in visually activated regions in Experiment 1, contrasting with a previous study (Richter et al., 2018).
results.evaluation: Claim C40 reports a negative finding that is important for interpretation. The absence of low-level visual area involvement in humans (contrasting with C24 citation to Richter et al., 2018) suggests that the current paradigm with minimal training (24 trials) and abstract labels promotes high-level symbolic processing rather than low-level perceptual associations. This is a valid negative result that helps distinguish the current findings from prior work.

results.result: The study demonstrates that reversibility of associations sharply differs between humans and non-human primates, with the interspecies difference in violation effects pointing to a more efficient species-specific learning system related to symbolic competence.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C109 represent the main conclusion integrating findings across both experiments and species. The sharp difference is supported by the consistent pattern: humans show reversibility in both experiments with no congruity × canonicity interactions, while monkeys show significant interactions indicating non-reversal in both experiments. The characterization as 'more efficient' and 'symbolic' is a reasonable inference from the data, though the mechanism remains speculative.

results.result: The human reversibility network extends beyond classical language areas to include bilateral homologs involved in music, dorsal areas involved in mathematics (MFG, IPS), and the VWFA. These areas correspond to regions with maximal cortical expansion and connectivity differences in humans versus other primates, suggesting multiple parallel brain networks possess symbolic abilities deployed across different domains (language, music, mathematics).
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C119 provide anatomical and theoretical interpretation of the human results. The bilateral activation (C110-C111) and dorsal extension (C112) are directly supported by the fMRI data. The VWFA involvement (C113) is confirmed by ROI analysis. The correspondence with regions of maximal human-primate differences (C115-C116) is supported by appropriate citations. The inference of multiple parallel symbolic networks (C119) is reasonable given the data, though it remains an interpretation rather than direct demonstration. The rejection of a single localized symbolic system (C118) is well-supported by the distributed bilateral activation pattern.

results.result: The study acknowledges a limitation of small sample size in monkeys (n=4 total, n=2 per experiment) compared to humans (n=55 total), which is common in primate studies but makes species-level extrapolation challenging. The authors addressed this by combining data from two different labs with two animals each.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 appropriately acknowledge a significant limitation. The small monkey sample size is a genuine concern for generalization, appropriately cited (C133, Fries and Maris, 2022). The two-lab replication strategy (C134) partially addresses this concern by demonstrating consistency across different animals, experimenters, and scanning environments. However, the limitation remains that only 2-3 monkeys per experiment is a small sample, and the results should be interpreted with this caveat.

results.result: The study acknowledges that interspecies differences could be due to hard-to-control factors including lifetime experiences and education in humans. However, the fact that 5-month-old human infants show similar symbolic reversibility effects suggests experiential factors may not fully explain the findings.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C136 appropriately acknowledge and address a major confound. The experiential difference between adult humans and lab-raised monkeys is a valid concern (C135). The counterargument citing infant data (C136, Kabdebon and Dehaene-Lambertz, 2019) is compelling but not definitive—infants still have 5 months of human-specific social and linguistic experience. This limitation is honestly presented, though it cannot be fully resolved within the current study design.

results.result: The introduction establishes the theoretical framework and prior evidence for the reversibility hypothesis. Symbolic thinking has been proposed as distinguishing humans from other primates, with bidirectional attachment as a key feature. Prior behavioral studies show non-human animals (bees, pigeons, macaques, baboons, chimpanzees) struggle to reverse learned associations, while humans as young as 8 months show spontaneous reversal. Previous neuroimaging studies in humans suggest involvement of the multiple-demand system, while monkey studies show learning effects restricted to sensory areas.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C26 provide the background and rationale for the study. These are primarily citations to prior work and are appropriately referenced. The characterization of prior findings is accurate based on the citations provided. The theoretical framework (C1-C2, C15) about symbolic bidirectionality is well-established in the literature. The summary of prior behavioral (C3, C16-C19) and neuroimaging (C20-C26) evidence appropriately motivates the current study's approach and hypotheses.

results.result: The discussion contextualizes the findings within prior literature and addresses methodological considerations. Previous behavioral studies found uniquely human spontaneous reversal, with reversibility proposed as a defining feature of symbolic reference. The current fMRI approach addresses limitations of behavioral studies by directly probing brain responses. The study design choices (minimal training, concrete objects, abstract labels, animals with speech experience) are justified relative to prior work showing that extensive training may lead to rigid low-level encoding.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C95 provide appropriate contextualization and methodological justification. The summary of prior behavioral work (C80-C87) is well-cited. The methodological rationale (C82-C83) for using fMRI to bypass behavioral confounds is sound. The discussion of occasional reversal reports in some animals (C84-C86) appropriately acknowledges complexity while maintaining the main conclusion. The comparison to prior training protocols (C89-C92) effectively justifies the current design choices. The justifications for stimulus choices (C93-C95) are reasonable.

results.result: The discussion reviews anatomical and functional differences between human and monkey brains. While many similarities exist, important differences include human brain size, arcuate fasciculus connectivity, prefrontal cortex volume, dendritic arborization, and synaptic density. Functionally, monkeys show feature tuning in prefrontal cortex unlike humans. Whether these anatomical differences underlie language learning differences remains controversial.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C107 provide appropriate anatomical context for interpreting the functional differences. The citations to comparative neuroanatomy (C101-C106) are extensive and appropriate. The acknowledgment that the anatomy-function relationship remains controversial (C107) is appropriately cautious. The observation about monkey PFC feature tuning (C100) is supported by the current data (Figures 1C, 4B) and prior literature. This contextualizes the sensory-level learning effects in monkeys.

results.result: The discussion proposes potential mechanisms for reversibility. Most learning rules are sensitive to temporal order, yet humans appear to forget temporal order at the symbolic level. Hippocampal replay in forward and reverse directions exists in both humans and animals, but this mechanism might have selectively expanded to symbol-related areas in the human brain.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C127 are largely speculative about mechanisms. The observation that humans 'forget' temporal order (C121) is an inference from the behavioral data but not directly tested. The proposal about hippocampal replay (C123-C127) is appropriately cited but remains a hypothesis for future work. The speculation that this mechanism expanded to symbolic areas in humans (C127) is reasonable but unsupported by the current data. These are appropriate speculations for discussion but should not be considered established findings.

results.result: The discussion notes that humans do not always disregard temporal order (e.g., alphabet), and that stimulus characteristics matter. The current study used abstract labels paired with concrete objects. In human infants, labels help construct object categories, and preverbal infants flexibly accept various stimuli as labels.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C131 provide appropriate nuance about the scope of the findings. The alphabet example (C128) appropriately acknowledges that reversibility is not universal. The description of stimulus design (C129) is accurate. The citations to infant label learning (C130-C131) appropriately contextualize the developmental trajectory and flexibility of symbolic learning. These claims appropriately bound the interpretation of the findings.

results.result: The discussion considers alternative interpretations and future directions. Monkeys can make multimodal associations for familiar individuals, though training typically uses simultaneous presentation. Even if specific circuits showed reversal in monkeys, humans may still differ in flexible arbitrary symbol association. The study suggests the human workspace may have acquired symbolic processing capacity during evolution. Future work should test chimpanzees, vocal learners, effects of social interaction, and potential critical periods.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C144 appropriately consider alternative interpretations and future directions. The acknowledgment of monkey multimodal abilities (C137) is appropriately cited and qualified. The speculation about workspace evolution (C139) is reasonable given the data but appropriately cautious. The suggestions for future work (C140-C143) are well-motivated and appropriately cited where relevant. The statement about the paradigm's utility (C144) is a reasonable conclusion.

results.result: In humans (Experiment 1), fMRI revealed that violations of learned auditory-visual associations activated a vast bilateral network including the multiple-demand system (IFG, MFG, AI, IPS, dACC), language network (left STS), and precuneus. Critically, this activation occurred equally for both canonical and reversed trial directions, with no significant interaction between congruity and canonicity, indicating spontaneous bidirectional reversal of associations.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accepted these findings as solid evidence for reversible associations in humans. Reviewer 1 stated the results are 'quite compelling' and that 'the data do support the hypothesis that humans are somewhat unique in their tendency to form reversible, symbolic associations.' Reviewer 2 described the findings as 'compelling results' and noted the manuscript is 'skillfully crafted.' The editor confirmed 'solid evidence in humans that helps elucidate the role of brain networks in symbolic processing.'

results.result: In monkeys (Experiment 1), after extended training (~960 trials per pair), fMRI showed congruity effects confined to early sensory areas (V1, V2, V4) and auditory association areas, occurring only in the canonical (learned) direction. No significant activation was found for reversed trials at the whole-brain level, and the interaction between congruity and canonicity was significant in V2 and V4, indicating lack of spontaneous reversal.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings with acknowledgment of methodological considerations. Reviewer 1 noted 'the results do appear to show that macaques show the predicted interaction effect (even despite the sample size), while humans do not. I think this is quite convincing.' Reviewer 3 acknowledged concerns about extended training but was satisfied by the authors' responses. The editor noted 'evidence from macaques was necessarily incomplete' due to 'hard-to-quantify differences in learning trajectories,' but did not reject the findings.

results.result: In monkeys (Experiment 2 with reward), significant canonical congruity effects were obtained after only 24 trials per pair, with activation in visual areas (V1, V2, V4) extending to prefrontal cortex (areas 45B, 46v, 6) and STS. The congruity effect was present only for high-reward conditions and remained restricted to the learned direction with no significant reversed congruity effect, replicating the lack of spontaneous reversal even with enhanced motivation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted Experiment 2 as addressing concerns from Experiment 1. Reviewer 2 stated 'the subsequent second experiment thoroughly addresses these concerns and effectively replicates the initial findings, thereby significantly strengthening the overall study.' Reviewer 3 was 'convinced by the responses' regarding training protocols. The faster learning and prefrontal involvement demonstrated that motivational factors did not explain the lack of reversal in monkeys.

results.result: In humans (Experiment 2 with visual-visual pairs), fMRI showed congruity effects in a network similar to Experiment 1 (bilateral MFG, left IPS, bilateral AI, dACC, left IT), though with limited language network involvement. Crucially, no interaction between congruity and canonicity was found, indicating humans encode visual stimulus pairs in a symmetrical, reversible fashion involving high-level cortical areas.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these findings as demonstrating reversibility extends beyond auditory-visual (language-like) associations. Reviewer 2 noted the experiment 'effectively replicates the initial findings' and Reviewer 3's concerns about language-specific effects were addressed. The finding that reversibility occurs with purely visual symbols strengthened the claim that this is a general symbolic capacity rather than language-specific.

results.result: Joint analysis of both human experiments revealed a main effect of congruity in bilateral regions (insula, MFG, precentral, IPS, precuneus, ACC, STS) significant in both canonical and reversed directions, with no region showing a congruity × canonicity interaction. Only left posterior STS showed a modality-specific effect (larger in auditory-visual than visual-visual), suggesting a broad bilateral network responds to violations of reversible symbolic associations regardless of modality.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this synthesis as demonstrating the generality of the reversibility effect across modalities. The finding of a single modality-specific region (pSTS) while the broader network remained consistent was viewed as supporting the authors' interpretation of a general symbolic network. No reviewer challenged these joint analysis findings.

results.result: ROI analysis using functional localizers showed main congruity effects in all ROIs (language areas, VWFA, right IT, multiple-demand regions). A congruity × experiment interaction was seen only in pSTS and IFG triangularis (larger effects in auditory-visual experiment), while no canonicity × congruity interaction was observed in any ROI, confirming whole-brain findings of full reversibility across both experiments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the ROI analysis findings. Reviewer 3 initially raised concerns about 'double-dipping' in statistical analyses but clarified this applied only to whole-brain results (Tables 1-4), not fROI results, and requested clarification rather than rejecting the findings. The ROI analysis provided converging evidence for the whole-brain results.

results.result: In Experiment 2, humans' behavioral familiarity ratings showed congruent reversed pairs were rated as significantly more familiar than incongruent reversed pairs and never-seen pairs (despite both being presented only 10% of trials), though less familiar than canonical pairs. A within-subject behavioral index of reversibility correlated with fMRI congruity effects in left area 44 and right cerebellum, confirming humans spontaneously reverse associations and experience a memory illusion of having seen reversed pairs.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these behavioral findings as supporting the fMRI evidence for spontaneous reversal. The correlation between behavioral and neural measures strengthened the interpretation. No reviewer challenged these results, and they were viewed as providing converging behavioral evidence for the neural findings.

results.result: The authors conclude that reversibility of associations sharply differs between humans and non-human primates, pointing to a more efficient species-specific learning system. The distributed bilateral activation in human prefrontal, temporal, and parietal cortices suggests the human workspace may have acquired a capacity to process arbitrary symbol systems during recent evolution.
results.evaluation: Reviewers expressed mixed views on the broader interpretive claims. Reviewer 3 extensively critiqued the framing, stating 'the framing is bigger than the finding' and that 'a key idea in this piece (that reversible symbolic inference is a singularity of the human brain) is being advanced rhetorically rather than empirically.' The reviewer noted the results 'only directly support a more modest claim (that macaques spontaneously reverse sequential associations less readily than humans do).' Reviewer 2 acknowledged 'this limitation is carefully addressed and discussed' but noted the sample size issue. The editor stated evidence from macaques was 'necessarily incomplete.'

results.result: The study acknowledges limitations including small monkey sample size (n=4 total, n=2 per experiment) and potential confounds from interspecies differences in experience and education. The authors note that combining data from two labs and the finding that 5-month-old human infants show similar reversibility effects partially address these concerns.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these limitations but had mixed views on their impact. Reviewer 1 stated 'an important strength of the results is that the critical finding is the presence of an interaction between congruity and canonicity in macaques, which does not appear in humans' and that 'the difference in sample size would be considerably more concerning' if results were reversed. Reviewer 2 noted 'the main limitation of the studies is the sample size of the non-human primate group (n=2 and n=3). Nevertheless, this limitation is carefully addressed and discussed.' Reviewer 3 raised concerns about 'hard-to-control factors' including 'a lifetime of open-field experiences and education' but was partially satisfied by reference to infant data.

results.result: The authors propose that a human-specific brain network may have evolved the capacity for reversible symbolic reference, and that multiple parallel and partially dissociable human brain networks possess symbolic abilities deployed in different domains (language, music, mathematics), rather than a single localized system being the primary engine of symbolic abilities.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 challenged the theoretical framing extensively, stating the extended network 'does not fit with the hypothesis that a single localised system, such as natural language or a universal generative faculty, is the primary engine of all human-specific abstract symbolic abilities' but noting this interpretation involves 'a debatable chain of assumptions.' The reviewer argued there is 'circularity in the framing whereby the authors say they are setting out to find out what is uniquely human, hypothesizing that the uniquely human thing is symbols, and then selecting a defining trait of symbols (spontaneous reversible association) *because* it seems to be uniquely human.' Other reviewers did not extensively comment on these theoretical claims.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers found the human reversibility findings (C4-C6, C35-C42) compelling and well-supported. Peer reviewers described results as 'quite compelling' and 'solid evidence,' matching OpenEval's SUPPORTED evaluation based on the fMRI data showing no congruity × canonicity interaction.

Strong agreement with methodological acknowledgment. Both found monkey non-reversal findings (C7-C8, C43-C48) convincing. OpenEval emphasized statistical evidence via interaction effects. Peer reviewers accepted findings as 'quite convincing' while acknowledging sample size and training considerations, which did not undermine their acceptance.

Strong agreement. Both evaluated reward-motivation experiment findings (C51-C58) as SUPPORTED. OpenEval noted the experiment addressed confounds about motivation. Peer reviewers stated it 'thoroughly addresses these concerns and effectively replicates the initial findings,' confirming that faster learning and prefrontal involvement did not enable reversal.

Strong agreement. Both found visual symbol reversibility findings (C59-C62, C64-C65) well-supported. OpenEval emphasized this extends beyond auditory-linguistic stimuli. Peer reviewers agreed it 'effectively replicates the initial findings' and addresses concerns about language-specific effects, supporting the general symbolic capacity interpretation.

Perfect agreement. Both accepted the joint analysis findings (C66-C70) demonstrating modality-general reversible symbolic network. OpenEval noted the single region (pSTS) showing experiment differences supports limited language-specific contributions. Peer reviewers accepted this synthesis without challenge.

Strong agreement. Both accepted ROI analysis findings (C71-C74) as providing convergent evidence. OpenEval emphasized the independent, subject-specific approach confirming whole-brain results. Peer reviewers did not challenge these findings; Reviewer 3's statistical concerns applied to whole-brain analyses, not ROI results.

Perfect agreement. Both found behavioral validation findings (C75-C79) well-supported. OpenEval emphasized the 'memory illusion' effect and brain-behavior correlations strengthening fMRI interpretation. Peer reviewers accepted these as providing converging behavioral evidence without challenge.

Significant disagreement on interpretive scope. OpenEval rated main conclusions (C108-C109) as SUPPORTED, viewing the sharp species difference as reasonable inference. Peer Reviewer 3 extensively critiqued the framing as 'bigger than the finding,' stating claims are 'advanced rhetorically rather than empirically' and results 'only directly support a more modest claim.' Editor noted evidence was 'necessarily incomplete.'

Partial agreement on sample size limitation (C132-C134). OpenEval rated as SUPPORTED with appropriate acknowledgment of limitation. Peer reviewers had mixed views: some found the interaction effect convincing despite small n, others noted it as a significant limitation. Reviewer 1 argued the critical interaction finding makes small sample less concerning than it would be for null results.

Partial agreement on experiential confounds (C135-C136). OpenEval rated as SUPPORTED, noting infant data counterargument is compelling but not definitive. Peer Reviewer 3 raised concerns about 'hard-to-control factors' including lifetime experiences but was partially satisfied by infant data reference. Both acknowledge this limitation cannot be fully resolved.

Disagreement on theoretical interpretation. OpenEval rated anatomical/theoretical claims (C110-C119) as SUPPORTED, finding the distributed bilateral network and rejection of single localized system well-supported. Peer Reviewer 3 challenged the theoretical framing extensively, noting 'debatable chain of assumptions' and potential circularity in defining symbols by uniquely human traits.
